reading.body:
CyrusOne's Lebanon, Ohio campus publishes 12 megawatts of IT capacity, the largest figure in Ohio, but it is one fifth of a statewide published total of 60.4 megawatts.

That statewide total covers only 8 of the 77 mapped Ohio facilities, so it is a floor rather than a census. Most Ohio data centers do not publish power figures at all, which means the state's apparent position in the national picture is unknown from this data. The 12 megawatts here is the top of a small published field, not evidence of a large one.

At 40 kilowatts per rack, a common AI training density, 12 megawatts supports roughly 300 racks. That is a modest footprint for AI training, and the 400,000 square feet of technical space implies a density well below what current AI halls run. The certifications, SOC 2 Type 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, FISMA, SSAE 16 Type II, and Green Globes, point to regulated enterprise workloads in healthcare, finance, and federal contexts rather than to AI training as the intended tenant.

What the data does not cover is decisive. Nothing is published about grid connection capacity at Lebanon, about expansion plans, or about current tenants. The suitability score of 58 lists announced expansion as its missing input, which is the right gap to name, because a 12 megawatt facility matters to AI scaling only if it can grow and only if the grid serving it can carry that growth.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
